The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of a system either increases or remains constant in any spontaneous process; it never decreases. plan.title: Entropy Explained
plan.description: Entropy is one of physics' most powerful ideas, yet most people misunderstand it. This video explains what entropy really is and why it gives time its direction.

beats.narration: Drop a cup and it shatters. But why does it never reassemble itself? The answer is one of the deepest ideas in all of physics.

props.clip_query: ceramic cup falling and breaking on floor
props.alt: a cup shattering on a hard floor in slow motion

beats.narration: That idea is entropy. Not just disorder, but something more precise: the number of microscopic ways a system can be arranged.

props.definition: A measure of how many microscopic arrangements, called microstates, correspond to the same observable state of a system.

beats.narration: Imagine four particles spread across two boxes. There is only one way to pack them all left, but six different ways to split them two and two.
The spread-out arrangement wins simply because it is far more probable. Entropy measures that probability. More microstates means higher entropy.

steps.note: S = entropy, W = number of microstates, k_B = Boltzmann's co

beats.narration: The second law of thermodynamics says entropy in an isolated system never decreases. Every spontaneous process moves toward the arrangement with the most microstates.

props.text: Entropy never decreases in an isolated system.

beats.narration: Heat always flows from hot to cold, never the reverse, because that direction increases entropy. The change in entropy equals heat transferred divided by temperature.

steps.note: Delta Q = heat added, T = temperature in Kelvin

beats.narration: This is why time feels one-directional. A shattered cup, melting ice, mixing gases: each moves toward more microstates and cannot spontaneously reverse.
Scientists call this the arrow of time. Entropy gives the universe a direction: from ordered, unlikely states toward disordered, probable ones.

props.clip_query: timelapse ice melting in a glass
props.alt: ice slowly melting into water in a clear glass

beats.narration: Entropy also limits every engine. No machine converts heat to work perfectly, because some energy always spreads into the surroundings, raising total entropy.
So entropy is not just disorder. It is probability made physical, the reason engines lose heat, ice melts, and time moves only forward.
Next time something breaks and does not fix itself, that is the second law at work. The universe always moves toward its most probable state.
